subtopic: REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MISSION TO LATIN AMERICA

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MISSION TO LATIN AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ministerial mission to Latin America returned to Ottawa on Wednesday of this week. I wish today to make a brief statement about the mission and its work, a mission which I am convinced marks a turning point in our relations with Latin America.
The house will recall that shortly before the mission left Canada the Prime Minister stated that its purpose was to assist the government in its review of policy toward Latin America, a part of the world with which we believe Canada should develop closer relations. The mission's main tasks were as follows: to explore the common benefits that might result from closer relations with Latin America; to explore all important aspects of Canada's relations with Latin America, political, economic and cultural; to demonstrate our desire to draw closer to Latin American countries on a bilateral basis and the importance we attach to our relations with the hemisphere as a whole; to enable ministers to have direct consultations with important Latin American leaders and to observe at first hand developments in some of the important Latin American countries; to review not only relations with Latin American countries but also world issues in which we and they have a common interest, and, to make Canada better known in Latin America, and to establish a basis for better understanding of Latin. America on the part of Canadians.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
The government felt that to accomplish these objectives it was necessary to send ministers who could speak with authority on matters of foreign policy, trade and economic questions and cultural affairs, supported by a
3294	COMMONS
Report on Mission to Latin America strong team of officials drawn from the departments and agencies of government principally concerned with our relations with Latin America. To gain a broad perspective on our relations with Latin America, the mission visited as many countries of that area as possible.
At one time or another five ministers took part in the mission. They were the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin); the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene); the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatchewan (Mr. Lang) with responsibilities in the field of industry, trade and commerce, and myself. My parliamentary secretary (Mr. Goyer) also took part. We so arranged our time that at least three of us were present in each country. In this way our three main areas of interest, political, economic and cultural, were always well covered.
Ministers were supported by senior officials of the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of the Secretary of State, as well as of the Canadian International Development Agency, the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, the Canada Council, the National Gallery, the National Film Board and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Most of these officials were with the mission throughout the tour.
The mission visited nine countries; six in South America-Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Peru and Venezuela; one in North America-Mexico-and two in Central America-Costa Rica and Guatemala. The tour lasted approximately one month. In each country ministers were received by the president and had a series of meetings with ministers of the host government. In most countries we talked with leading members of the legislative bodies and with some representatives of regional and international organizations. Certain officials had individual meetings or made brief side visits, sometimes to neighbouring countries not covered by the official itinerary. In all these meetings a very wide range of subjects was discussed in considerable depth.
In the political field we discussed hemispheric questions and current international issues. In the trade and economic field we discussed trade in the multilateral context, bilateral trade, financing and investment. Everywhere we went we found that development is a main preoccupation of government.

DEBATES	November 29, 1968
In the cultural sphere, to which the Latin Americans also attach great importance, we explored a wide spectrum of activities ranging from scientific research to film production. I would like to emphasize that our discussions related to concrete possibilities as much as to general policies and procedures.
While we worked mainly with governments we paid special attention to private institutions which, both in Latin America and in Canada, have an important role to play in developing our relations. We had meetings, for example, with chambers of commerce, with university rectors, with museum directors and leading experts in the arts. We met with Canadian businessmen and with Canadian missionaries, religious and lay, and with other volunteer workers. In all these meetings we were greatly impressed by the importance of the part which private individuals and groups can play in the pursuit of goals shared by the peoples of Canada and Latin America.
In every country we visited we were offered a warm and most hospitable reception. The atmosphere in our talks was at all times cordial, frank and, as a rule, quite informal. The scope and frequently the depth of our exchanges were striking; we entered into a dialogue which we intend to continue.
Our mission was widely publicized in all the countries visited. Good coverage was afforded by the press as well as by radio and television stations. I can assure the house that the presence of the mission was felt in Latin America.
There is one feature of the mission which I would like to mention. The mission was an excellent projection abroad of the Canada of today. Almost every member of the mission was bilingual in French and English. In addition many could speak Spanish or Portuguese.
The mission has amassed a great deal of valuable information and has formed impressions and tentative opinions which will clearly be of great assistance to the government when completing its review of relations with Latin America. The substantial preparations for the mission and the work of the mission itself constituted the first phase of that review, and much has been accomplished in this first phase. Some projects which can be advanced under present policies and procedures have been identified; a few of these have been carried to completion and the others will be followed up without delay.
One example is the establishment of a joint Mexico-Canada committee for the consideration of matters of common interest to the two
November 29, 1968	COMMONS
countries in the political, economic and commercial fields. The committee may also consider other matters such as, for example, cultural relations. With the leave of the house, I wish now to table, in English and in French, the note on this subject which I signed and handed to the foreign minister of Mexico when the ministerial mission was in that country. This note and the note which the foreign minister signed and handed to me in reply constitute an agreement establishing the committee.

1 am glad to be able to report that the mission accomplished the objectives set by the Prime Minister before its departure. It is the desire of the government to determine, in the shortest possible time, how present possibilities may be translated into action within the framework of our broader foreign policy review. The members of the ministerial mission will now reflect on what they have found and seen and heard and will shortly make a report to the government.
I would like to make clear that it is the intention of the government, before completing its review of policy toward Latin America, to consult individuals and groups within the Canadian community which have an interest in Latin America and, in parliament, to submit the review to critical examination in committee. In this process the government will welcome presentations and representations from all sides. I would add that the ministerial mission itself has given a new impetus to the development of Canadian relations with the countries of Latin America.
I am sure I speak on behalf of all members of this house when I once again express to the governments and peoples of the countries we visited our sincere thanks and deep appreciation for the reception they accorded to the ministerial mission. To the governments and peoples of the countries of Latin America which the mission was not able to visit I would like to say that in undertaking our voyage in Latin America, we were extending the hand of friendship to them also.
I would like to take this opportunity to express my warm appreciation, and that of all members of the mission, for the excellent arrangements made for us by our own embassies in the capitals we visited. Their

subtopic: REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MISSION TO LATIN AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all welcome the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the various ministers who accompanied him and their officials back to Canada from what was obviously a most arduous trip. I hope the ministers had a chance to look behind the glamour and glitter of some of the countries they visited and see some of the serious problems resulting from the population explosion and severe poverty. We shall be interested in studying the implications of the visit in the fields of expanded trade and commerce, energy, cultural exchanges, external affairs, and so on. We also hope the details of the real effects of the mission will soon be made public in an ongoing policy review.
We should be interested to know whether increases in trade can be expected, what problems would accompany or impede such increase, and whether Canada ought to set up permanent structures in those countries in Latin America to facilitate trade. We share the government's views about the usefulness of an expansion of cultural relations, and here again we must wait and see what are the implications of this exchange.
In the fields of external relations and aid to South America the questions that come to mind are these. What role can our country best play; what role will we play vis-a-vis the United States in South America; and has Canada selected certain South American
3296	COMMONS
Report on Mission to Latin America countries upon which to concentrate aid? Another question is, how is aid to South America to be integrated with Canada's overall aid policy? We were interested to hear that following a proposal of the government led by my right hon. friend from Prince Albert an agreement has been signed between Canada and Mexico. We shall be interested in the membership of this new committee.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
The minister did not specifically mention the Organization of American States, but obviously during any visit by Canadians to South America this must have been very much in mind. Here may I enter a caveat. I hope the Canadian government will continue to be sceptical about accepting the full implications of membership in this organization. As I see them these implications are in the category of defence, and they have political overtones as well. If we join the O.A.S. we shall become part of a hemispheric defence system with all this would involve for Canada. We should therefore need to know, as the review progresses, of the political conditions Canada would accept for membership in the organization. Would we be prepared, as Mexico has been on certain occasions, to pursue a course independent of the O.A.S. and suffer the economic consequences of such independence?
I hope there will be wide public discussion of these issues; that platitudes about dialogue, studies in depth and so on will be ended, and that the people will be told exactly what are the implications of any move to join what now appears to some of us to be a rather reactionary organization.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MISSION TO LATIN AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Fundy-Royal I think there is much more that the Secretary of State for External Affairs could have told us. But I suppose we shall have to settle for two promises; one, that there will be a further report on this mission; and two, that at some point the whole subject of our relations with Latin America will be referred to parliament or to a committee of this house.
Frankly, what we have been given this morning, while very interesting, was little more than a travelogue. This certainly applies to the statement the minister made while he was on his feet. As for the document he asked leave to table, copies of which have been made available to some of us, I find it includes a long list of all the lunches and

DEBATES	November 29, 1968
receptions which the ministers attended, and really it contains no more than the minister told us.
However, there has been a promise of a further report. I hope there will be more substance in it, and I hope, too, that this question of our relations with the countries of the western hemisphere will be referred to parliament, referred to a committee, and adequately discussed before any final decisions are taken. I need not take the time of the house to suggest what the solutions to these problems are; because, as the hon. member for Fundy-Royal has been saying, the whole question of our trading relationship with the countries of the western hemisphere is highly important to us and we feel that in the world today with its problems of over-population, its economic problems, its socio-economic problems, not forgetting the need for aid all over the world, there is a special role which Canada can play by way of aid to certain sections of the western hemisphere.
I think this should be brought out of the sphere of things that are awfully vague. It should be pinned down. We should know what we are doing.
I also want to say we are aware of the fact that lurking behind all this talk, all this travelogue, is the question of the Organization of American States to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs made no reference whatever. There is no reference in the formal statement, or that I can find in the multi-page document that has been tabled. This too is something we feel parliament should have an opportunity to discuss before we have been taken down the path to a situation that might involve us in defence, monetary and trading relations that would make us more a satellite than we are now of the main power in the Organization of American States.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the minister has taken time on motions to give us an interesting travelogue. We have enjoyed it, but the fact is that there are matters of substance to which this parliament must give its attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) gave us this morning a most interesting report on what seems to have been a wonderful jaunt to Latin America for him and his colleagues, and very little to show for it.
November 29, 1968

The newspapers tell us that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), who also made the trip to Latin America, allegedly stated that it was an "exploratory trip" and it was not undertaken in order to sign trade agreements, or even cultural agreements.
Listening to the Secretary of State for External Affairs a while ago, I noted that the ministerial mission had taken a great interest in the development of the film industry and related activities in Latin America. I do not know if the film industry is as well organized in Latin America as in Hollywood, for instance, but in any case, it seems to me that a month of talks, visits, cocktails and banquets should allow us to hope that Canada, through the agreements that will be reached as a result, will try to meet the repeated requests made by representatives of Latin America to some countries other than the United States, because a study of history shows that instead of encouraging the development of Latin America, the United States has enslaved those countries.
Appeals were made at the 56th conference of the Interparliamentary Union held in Lima and recently at a symposium held at Laval University in Quebec, where President Luis Alberto Sanchez stated that integration must be the aim of Latin America. He recalled that, for years, countries had sought the disunion of Latin American states and having defeated them, not only from the outside but from the inside, they managed to enslave and exploit them. In one of his speeches, President Sanchez stated:
Because of the poverty, aggravated by a lack of a proportionate quantity of consumer goods, by their high cost in relation with the low salaries, by the excessive growth of the population-
Which is said to be 3 per cent in Latin America.
-the excessive concentration of capital in the hands of a few people and in capitalistic areas, the pressure exerted by the exasperated and the desperate increases, and they fall prey easily to national and foreign propaganda in favour of communism and fascism, both of which are international anti-American doctrines.
Mr. Speaker, in the light of a statement like that one from a representative of one of the Latin American states, I feel that the trade relations which Canada wishes or intends to establish with those Latin American countries should encourage their development.
We are giving considerable help to the underdeveloped countries and Latin America

On Tuesday I asked the Prime Minister a question about government policy with regard to the authorization of ministers of the crown to express their personal opinions concerning policies being formulated. The right hon. gentleman said in part in his answer, which appears at page 3188 of Hansard, that a minister in answering must make sure he does not place himself in an irrevocable position which might be contrary to that which the government might eventually take.
That night I had the pleasure of observing the Postmaster General on a national television interview. I took note of what he said. On the last sitting day, Wednesday, I then asked the Prime Minister the following question which appears at page 3275 of Hansard:
Would the right hon. gentleman say whether the statements made by the Postmaster General on national television last night, that Canada should get out of NATO as well as NORAD since we have no contribution to make in that field, meets with the earlier guide line the Prime Minister laid down-

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I did not say that.
The fact is, as confirmed by what is purported to be an official transcript of the proceedings, that the Postmaster General in this interview was asked the following questions and made the following replies:
Pape: You made statements in the past that you felt that we should get out of NORAD as well as NATO and I'd like to ask you about that.
Kierans: This hasn't come up in cabinet, thank the Lord ... (laughs)-

Mr. Chairman, there are so many aspects of the work of the minister and his department upon which I should like to comment that I will have to exercise a great deal of restraint in the choice of topics. It is not my wish to trespass for too long on the time of the committee but there are certain particular questions concerning the attitudes and the judgment of the minister which I feel it is necessary to raise. I hope the minister will excuse my being very blunt in some of my remarks, as I view with a good deal of concern some of the tendencies which are all too apparent.
I have already found occasion to comment as frankly as I can upon the credibility gap arising from the discrepancy in the assurance which the minister, in another capacity, gave this house and the country in connection with the expenditures of the current year. I have expressed my condemnation of the assurance given to bondholders through the securities and exchange commission of the United States. I described this behaviour as inexcusable and condemned it in the strongest possible terms on one occasion when the minister was not in the house-and he seemed to think I had taken advantage of his absence in doing so. I repeated this charge in the minister's presence. As far as I know he has never felt it necessary to give any explanation to the house or to a committee of the house as to the reasons for his behaviour or in justification of what transpired.
I say again that the minister and others responsible in the government misled the house. Maybe they feel that because they have a majority here they are not bound to give an answer, that there is no need for them to account to the house or to the Canadian people. I am not one who uses words like "arrogance" readily, but I think the minister owes this committee some explanation of the failure of the government to live up to its assurances, or of its action in misleading the House of Commons and the Canadian public, for it can only be described as that. The Canadian people did not give this government a majority in parliament in order to permit it to ignore charges or fail to account to the people for its behaviour. This is not good enough.
I want to talk for a while today about the budget resolutions but not for the purpose of discussing the merits of the resolutions as such. We shall have a further opportunity, I realize, to discuss the iniquitous 2 per cent social development tax together with the other measures which the government has put

November 29, 1968
Supply-Finance
forward. Today I wish to comment on one group of the budget measures. Again, we shall have an opportunity later to discuss these on their merits. I wish to comment on a particular problem which the Minister of Finance has placed before the Canadian people by the manner in which he is proceeding. I believe this is another indication of something approaching callousness and indifference or, indeed, injustice on the part of the minister and the government. I am referring to the changes which were proposed in connection with inheritance and gift taxes.
Inheritance taxes were formerly of concern mainly to a relatively small group of the well-to-do. Now, with the proposed reductions in the exemptions, they will be of real concern to hundreds of thousands of Canadians, a substantial proportion of the people of this country. This situation arises not only because of the lowering of the exemptions but also because of the continuing inflation which exists. The minister said he wanted to help transfers to be made between husbands and wives by exempting them from transfer tax, gift tax or inheritance tax. In the process of doing so he has proposed to make it infinitely more difficult for a son or a daughter to help a parent or for a family to maintain a family farm or a family business. There can be no doubt about this.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
The new rates will make it virtually impossible for a family to maintain control of a substantial family business, a large family business. This, of course, is bound to lead to more U.S. takeovers and this sort of thing, but we will have an opportunity to speak about this when the measure is specifically before us. But there are thousands and thousands of thrifty Canadians who, through the course of their lives, have built up farms. In the past they have been able to arrange the transfer of their farms over a period of time through a farmer-son partnership or something of that sort, and now the Minister of Finance proposes to make that pretty well impossible in the future, or at least to create much difficulty.
There is a lot of talk about maintaining the family farm. There is also a lot of emphasis on the need for maintaining the efficiency of family farms for them to be competitive. Yet obviously the minister is making it much more difficult for a family farm to maintain its capital position and remain in a viable state. Certainly this measure strikes a heavy blow at the concept of the family farm, and a

heavy blow at the efforts of anybody who has built up a small business to keep it in his family in any satisfactory condition.
I only mention these details today for the purpose of emphasizing the importance of the subject that I now propose to develop. I have done this to emphasize that what I am talking about concerns not only a few wealthy people in Canada but indeed hundreds of thousands of Canadians. We will have plenty of time to discuss the details of the legislation, but my point today is that legislation which the minister announced, I think it was on October 12, the date of his budget speech-I do not want to be wrong about this date but I think it was approximately October 12-has not yet been introduced and there is no sign of it. As far as we know it will not be made public until some time in the new year. My point, and I want to make it as emphatically as I can, is that this legislation which is to take effect as of October 12 will not have been seen by anybody in October, November or December, and I do not know about January of next year.
Here is legislation that affects the plans, the wills and the intentions of hundreds of thousands of Canadians, and yet the Minister of Finance for some reason apparently thought it was perfectly all right for him to announce on October 12 that these changes are going to be made and leave hundreds of thousands of Canadians hanging in limbo for months and months and months.
Shame.

The minister says he is anxious to try to help transfers between husbands and wives. I cannot help but notice the comments that experts have been making on the budget resolution, its lack of clarity in a number of respects, the confusion it has created, and the fact that nobody will know where they really are until the legislation is introduced, in fact, until it becomes law.
In the meantime everybody is hanging in limbo. I do not know what is going to happen, what the position is of people who have had the misfortune to die or will die between the time the minister made his announcement and the time the law becomes effective. I do not know what anybody can do in the meantime to try to protect himself with regard to this measure. Lawyers and others are making it very clear that they are finding it exceedingly difficult to give anybody any advice. The one thing they are saying is that a very substantial percentage of Canadians will have to

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, before lunch I was explaining to the committee the confusion and injustice created by the Minister of Finance as a result of the imprecise manner in which he proceeded to announce the changes in gift and estate taxes. I should like to continue on this quiet Friday afternoon to give the Minister of Finance the benefit of another view in respect of one or two other aspects. I mentioned this morning that the budget speech was delivered on October 12. I believe it was delivered on October 22 and I should like to be as accurate as possible.
There appears to be an indication that for three or four months we will be uncertain about these taxes because of the content of the legislation concerned. In respect of anything that is far reaching we may experience several years of uncertainty so far as judicial interpretation is concerned. I do not intend to complain about the judicial doubts at the moment but rather about the procedure the minister has followed which in turn has created serious confusion in the minds of not just thousands but hundreds of thousands of Canadians. This is inexcusable.
It is my hope that the minister will not attempt to justify the creation of this confusion by saying how difficult it is to get measures before the house. I do not think there is any question of emergency in this regard. The minister has said that as far as revenue and expenditures are concerned things will pretty well balance out, at least so far as this aspect of his budget speech is concerned. I refer, of course, to the changes in estate and inheritance taxes.
The minister obviously chose his own time to announce these changes in the law. They should not be judged in terms of revenue but rather in terms of their effect on the Canadian people. Perhaps the minister introduced these changes at this time to distract attention from the size of the budget deficit and the general increase in taxation. Certainly he has created not only additional but enormous confusion.

November 29, 1968
Supply-Finance
I am wondering how estates of individuals who have died since the minister's budget speech are being administered. What effect is this uncertainty having in respect of insurance policies payable to widows and children? I am sure the situation cannot be exactly felicitous at the moment. Having announced these changes, the minister ought to have proceeded immediately to bring them into effect, thereby eliminating this confusion and bringing assistance to these widows as quickly as possible. If the minister intended to wait several months, why did he include the element of retroactivity?
The size of gifts that could be made free of taxation under the law as it existed prior to October 22 was not substantial. No great harm could befall if citizens were able to operate under the old laws so far as exemptions were concerned. Those Canadians who might have chosen to make large gifts in order to benefit from the old rates could possibly do so during this interval. This situation could have been covered by making the new rates retroactive so far as gift taxes were concerned.
As I pointed out this morning, I do not think the minister or the government fully realized the effect these proposals would have on institutions such as the family farm. Quite apart from these effects, I do not think there is any real justification for this retroactive feature regarding testamentary provisions. Certainly, even under this government, nobody is going to be in a hurry to die just to get the benefits of certain tax rates which will prevail for a limited period of time.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I suggest that the proper procedure to follow with regard to a measure designed to reform taxation-and the minister put this forward as an interim measure of reform- would be to introduce a draft bill for study and clarification because when we are considering measures which have to be fitted into the total tax structure in order to see how they work out there are all sorts of complexities that even the minister and his staff are not likely to see at first glance. So I suggest that the proper course would be to have some procedure whereby people could express their views and which would elicit comments from others outside the government service who have to work and live with these laws from day to day.
I suggest this is an improvised reform. We had improvised estimates last winter that

proved to be very wide of the mark despite the most firm assurances concerning their validity. Now we have an improvised reform introduced in such a way that there will be the most severe confusion for months at least and maybe irremediable hardship for some people who get caught in the meantime.
The minister has put this measure forward as one which will be of assistance to wives. It may in the end assist wives after the confusion has passed but it will certainly assist one group of people, namely lawyers, because it will result in wills being drafted and perhaps redrafted by the thousands if not by the hundreds of thousands.
The minister has taken this course and has created confusion. I say to him that the best thing he can do now to minimize the difficulties that exist and help the Canadian people get out of the mess he has created is to immediately produce the draft bills-because more than one is required-and to place before the house and the people of the country the detailed legislation. I hope the minister does have the legislation ready. I think he should no later than Monday place before members of the house and the country draft legislation so that at least some of the confusion resulting from the bare bones of the budget resolutions will be removed and the process of consideration and analysis of the legislation can be started.
The week end is approaching so I will be content to wait until the first day of the week when I would most earnestly call upon the minister to circulate among the members of the house draft legislation relating to these proposals. The legislation must be ready inasmuch as a month ago, on October 22, the minister announced his changes. Let us have it in draft form so that we can at least start to remove the confusion which exists.
I should now like to turn briefly to two other areas. I wish to express my concern, regarding the attitude which the Minister of Finance has adopted toward the country and the provinces with regard to financial questions in general. I will not go over the ground which I covered in the budget debate but I again call the minister's attention to the effect his stand will have upon the pending priorities in the country, the effect it will have on increasing the disparity in services in various parts of the country, and the unfortunate effect his attitude will have on federal-provincial relations. I am referring to the minister's imposition of restraints and at the same time his tendency to push the provinces into new programs. Generally speaking, I do not
November 29, 1968

want to exaggerate, but I think there is a very real danger that in a short period of time this government, through the medium of the Minister of Finance as well as the Prime Minister, will cause a serious deterioration in federal-provincial relations and will very rapidly lead the country close to disaster in this area.
I urge the minister to change his approach in another area which I will mention briefly. I refer to his attitude toward the problems of international currency. Judging from the minister's public pronouncement I think he is unbelievably complacent with regard to these problems because he has given the Canadian people the impression that last week's problem was largely one of European concern. His statement may have been intended to give reassurance about the strength of the Canadian dollar but the fact is we in Canada are immediately affected by the restrictions which Great Britain has imposed upon trade as a result of the currency difficulties. Surely we must all be very concerned about the way that various countries are reacting to these currency difficulties by adopting policies of restriction which cannot help but have a dampening effect upon international trade and which, if they spread, could lead to a very serious increase in the difficulties in international commerce.
I think the minister should be taking initiatives to try to bring about measures to strengthen the international currency system, and he should be doing this not only through his officials. I think there is no country in the world that has a greater interest in this or has more to fear from the existing situation than has Canada, despite the assurances of the minister. I say this because it must be very clear to every Canadian that, for example, every time the United States feels it necessary to take some particular measure to project their currency position, that measure is likely to have an effect on Canada because of the extent of our trade with the United States. When the United States imposes particular measures of a restrictive nature to preserve its cash position, what usually happens is that the Minister of Finance has to beetle off down to Washington to get an exemption from that restriction and thus yields a further measure of Canadian independence.
It is pretty well accepted that as a result of efforts we made in 1963 and again last winter to get an exemption from the United States
Supply-Finance
we really do not have any independent monetary policy left in Canada. I am not exaggerating. The minister can make a face about it, but the fact is that as a result of the extent to which we are tied in by the arrangements we have with the United States in this respect, our effective autonomy in the area of an independent monetary policy is very limited. It seems to me that every time there is a monetary crisis which affects the United States or ourselves there is a very real chance it will result in a further diminution of our independence as a country.
In addition, there is our general interest in doing everything we can in Canada through our international associates to try to achieve happier methods than we have today of providing for an orderly adjustment of currencies as required, and not just have countries resorting to the kind of restrictive practices to which they are resorting today which, as I said, when they involve the United States and ourselves usually result in some reduction of our independent position. I say to the minister, therefore, there is no country that has more reason than Canada to be concerned about this subject. When he gives the Canadian people the impression that the existing difficulty is not of much concern to us but is primarily a European concern, I suggest to him he is doing no service to Canada in taking this line.

The other day, Mr. Chairman, the Globe and Mail contained a report of an interview or discussion between Jay Walz, correspondent of the New York Times, Seymour Topping, foreign news editor of the New York Times, and the Prime Minister of this country. The Prime Minister was asked the following question:
Are you worried by the influx of U.S. capital investment, in the sense that this investment might result in an American economic domination of this country?
In reply the Prime Minister stated:
I think the problem of economic domination is somewhat inevitable-not only of the United States over Canada but perhaps over countries of Europe as well.
We have long suspected that the Liberal party had committed itself to continental integration, that the Liberal party has no concern about the future of Canadian nationalism, and this statement of the Prime Minister confirms our worst fears. I am not standing here today with the objective of haranguing the Minister of Finance. I said what I did to gain the minister's attention. I wanted his attention because I want to ask him some questions rather than to stand here and say I have all the answers, that I can tell him how to run the country. I should like to pose some questions to the Minister of Finance and to the members on that side of the house.
Perhaps the minister has some answers to these questions. After all, there are some members who recall some of the statements made by the present Minister of Finance when he was on the opposition benches. At that time we had reason to hope that things would be different if he became minister of finance. After all, he was the white hope of Walter Gordon; this was the man the former minister of finance felt had a genuine interest in the future survival of this country. This is the man who, from the opposition benches, denounced those forces that were working against Canadian nationalism. Today he is a powerful figure; he is the Minister of Finance. He sits in that exalted place and he has enormous influence in terms of the policies this

country will be following, the kind of objectives that will be sought through the use of budgetary policies.
I ask the minister if he agrees with that statement by the Prime Minister, whether he believes that Canada is doomed to extinction, that it is inevitable our economy will be dominated by the United States? Does he believe that if it is dominated by the United States there can be such a thing as Canadian independence, that we can pursue social policies different from those directed by the United States?

I am not going to take a definitive stand on the question of foreign ownership. I am not at all convinced that what stands in the way of Canada developing her own policies or maintaining her independence is foreign ownership. I think that excuse is too glib and too simple and I do not buy it at all. I think that what is standing in the way is the refusal of the government to stand up to corporate power, whether it be Canadian, American, British or any other corporate power, and to say that the government of Canada as elected by the people of this country should decide the nature and scope of our society, that our lives are not going to be ruled by the makers of toothpaste and underarm deodorant.
Policies should be formulated by this parliament rather than in the board rooms of corporations. Our policies must be debated by this parliament rather than foisted upon us by faceless corporations. We must declare that taxation will originate in this parliament instead of our being subjected to the kind of taxation that is imposed upon us by corporate power. Let us make no mistake about that, Mr. Chairman. Our corporations tax Canadians just as effectively as does the government, perhaps more effectively because Canadians do not always see such taxation whereas they do see taxation by government. The corporations, aided and abetted by our tax system, decide on the kind of expenditures they are going to make and the kind of policies they will pursue. As a result of our tax system all of us pay for this, whether we buy the specific products of the corporations or not.
I am prepared to sit down at this moment, Mr. Chairman, if the minister would tell me whether he believes that this country is inevitably doomed to economic domination by the United States. Does the minister wish to answer at this time?

The simple answer is, no.

What we want to know, Mr. Chairman, is what sort of policies the government is going to bring in to ensure that this is not allowed to happen. We want to know what sort of commitment the government is going to make to the Canadian people that this will not happen.
We live in great fear of retaliation. Liberal after Liberal has risen in this house and across the country, including no less a Liberal than the former prime minister, Mr. Pearson, and spoken of this fear. Mr. Pearson made a speech in the west in which he intimated that in this country we really cannot have an independent policy because 60 per cent of our exports go to the United States. He asked how we can maintain our independence when we have so many eggs in the one basket.
We seem to have this great fear that the United States will do dreadful things to us if we try to assert ourselves, if we try to develop a policy in regard to NATO that is suitable to Canada, or a policy in regard to NORAD, or if we make a move to recognize China before the United States is ready to grant us permission. There is a fear that we cannot do any of these things, and this despite the rather enlightened statements made by those who ran in the last election. Now that these same gentlemen are in office their statements seem to be forgotten; certainly they are not reflected in government policy.
What are we afraid of? It seems to me that the United States needs Canada infinitely more than Canada needs the United States. This talk of retaliation is really just a bit of nonsense. I have gone over this in my own mind and have tried to visualize in what way the United States could retaliate in any real fashion that would be of long run significance to us, and I have failed to find such ways. It seems to me that the great power of the United States rests in the chicken heart of the government and is not based on sound economic grounds. If the United States chose to invade Canada, of course, or to send a military force across the border, I do not think there is much question in my mind or anybody else's mind that that would be the end

of the ball game. But I doubt that we need worry about that sort of thing because I do hot think the United States is really interested in retaliation of that kind. What we are discussing here is economic retaliation.
In this regard, Mr. Chairman, what can the United States really do to us? Would they stop buying our iron ore? They need it. Not only that, but in some ways they have given us a hostage to fortune in the sense that so much of our raw material resources are owned by the United States. They would hurt themselves in two ways. I suggest that those who are afraid that the United States would stop buying from Canada are really scaring us with an empty threat. The Paley report of some years ago pointed out that the United States would become increasingly dependent on raw materials from abroad, particularly from Canada. Therefore, I think we can assert our independence and can take a stand without any great fear of retaliation.
Sometimes, Mr. Chairman, ministers of finance have a phobia about capital flows, about our money supply from the United States being cut off. Actually, all of the evidence seems to indicate that we are almost completely self-sufficient in this country in the matter of capital formation. If we are not completely so at the present time we could make ourselves self-sufficient if we taxed foreign corporations as adequately as the Carter commission suggested they should be taxed. Much of the potential taxation that is not collected in this country is money that is of benefit to foreign corporations.
As the result of this fear about the inflow of United States capital being cut off, Canada has made all sorts of suicidal arrangements that restrict our ability to influence monetary policy in this country. We probably agreed to a fixed exchange rate in return for access to the United States capital market. The Liberal party prides itself on being businesslike. It likes to talk of the close relationship that exists between it and the chamber of commerce. The chamber of commerce is enthralled with it. But it strikes me that the Liberals are poor businessmen and have made bad deals for the nation.
The other day during the debate on defence production I was pleased to be told that we do not have to worry about the end of the war in Viet Nam. If that war comes to an end

and some of the defence production sharing agreements we now have with the United States are not renewed, the factories of Canada can switch over to other kinds of production. I was pleased to get that information because I think we should be getting out of shared cost defence agreements with the United States. I think the government should stop scaring the working people of this country into believing that we have to stay with these agreements because there is $300 million worth of work involved, as though no other work were available. It is as though these people are to be committed to making bombs and bullets used to kill people in a war we do not approve of, in a war in which our government has remained neutral.

Is it right for the government to slant its words in this direction? Is it right for the government to say to the Canadian people, when some of us ask for military production to be stopped because we do not wish to participate, even by the making of armaments, in a war we do not approve of: Oh, but we are preserving your jobs; that is why armaments must be made; your jobs must be preserved. I think it is quite dreadful for the government to take this stand and I hope the minister will take the opportunity to comment on this situation.
It seems to me that nature was very good to Canada. It gave us enormous wealth and great opportunity. I think Canada was very fortunate in its early leaders, who knew that to create a nation with a different sense of values they would need to be imaginative, bold and strong. Our early Canadian leaders overcome the obstacles of distance and geography and welded our nation on the northern part of this continent. They could easily have said: The economic lines on this continent flow north and south, and abdicated their responsibilities. But they did not. They made enormous sacrifices to create a special kind of country and they were successful. Distances were overcome, the nation survived, and it has prospered. But just at a time when the prophecy of another statesman who said that the 20th century will belong to Canada may come true, we find that the Prime Minister and the government do not believe the prophesy; they do not believe it will come true and do not believe it needs to come true.
This house is entitled to answers from the government. We want to know what sort of fiscal and financial policies generally the government will bring in to make sure we are

masters of our own house and that the people of this country have a future. I do not think we need to pay, as some on the government side have suggested, a large price for our independence. If anything, our independence ought to make us more prosperous than we now are. Although this debate cannot continue for much longer I look forward to hearing the minister say something on this subject that will assure our people we have not been sold out completely, as the words of the Prime Minister would indicate.

Mr. Chairman, at the very beginning of my remarks, I would like to say that economic balance is impossible in the present context without financial reform.
Recently, I attended the meetings of the United Nations, which must face up to the communist expansion in the world. In order to do that, we have no solution other than to arm ourselves to the teeth and ask every member country for a bigger contribution.
On the other hand, at the meeting of the economic committee, of which I was a member, I said that in order to fight communism, we should not resort to weapons or force, because I think we shall not defeat communism by using force against force.
In fact, communism is an idea and an idea must be fought with another idea, stronger, deeper, more logical, easier to understand and better suited to the economic objectives and realities of each country.
The outcome of all that is that more money is asked to revive the arms race, to buy more arms and stockpile more war material, to face the communist threat throughout the world.
There again it has been found that everything is simply an economic and financial matter, each country knuckles under again and wonders how to finance its contribution and discharge its commitments. Everything depends on each country's finances.
So, I simply said to my colleagues: If you want to finance your military organizations, if you want all countries to contribute adequately and according to their responsibilities, you must set up a financial organization which will enable every country to contribute its share, if there are no other means, without depriving the people of the necessities.
Here in Canada, we have a huge debt which cripples all our initiatives, all our economic activities. We pay too much interest on money. Federal and provincial debts are

immeasurable, as well as municipal, school
and individual debts.
We are now at a stage where we can no longer pay the interest on our debts; however, we must find billions of dollars to cope with communism, to organize ourselves and meet our commitments.
If we cannot meet our obligations reasonably well under the present system, let us try to improve it, let us try to find a few practical solutions to balance our economy again. If building destructive machinery is physically possible, it should also be financially possible. Something that is physically possible, should logically be possible, financially and economically. This is the point I want to make.
I should like to go over what has been done since June 25, since the present government has come to power. The claim is that great things have been done. But I say, that the people are being more and more dispossessed, and that they have new economic and financial problems. That is what the present administration has brought.
How is it that thinkers, free men like the members of the government should suddenly become the slaves of the old routines, customs and disciplines of the Liberal party? This was supposed to have been something new. They were supposed to have found a new organization to balance the economy without increasing taxes. They were supposed to find financial ways and all. Nothing at all that has been done.
A series of reforms were made in the departments, and in the office staff of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). That is not at all where reforms should be made. The people are not lacking anything there. But they do in private homes, residences and slums.
Since the present government has come to power, interest rates have been increased. Those who used to receive from 2.75 per cent to 5 per cent will get 6 per cent, 7 per cent and even more in the future, from $15 to $30 more per $1,000, from $15,000 to $30,000 per million. The poverty of the millionnaires, or lesser capitalists, does not need to be abolished. There is something more pressing than that, like increasing family allowances from $6 or $8 a month to a reasonable level, commensurate with the increase in the national production and the increase in the cost of living.
Up to $60 per month and sometimes $120 per month is distributed to foster homes and

Supply-Finance
orphanages for children of the same age. Can an unmarried person understand that?
The government does not lack money, but residences and private homes do. However, public administration goes on as before, increasing the expenses of departments and distributing increasingly considerable sums to political parties, while the individuals lack money.
The government members are constantly increasing the income of citizens who already have one thanks to their employment or their capital, but they fail to increase the income of citizens who do not have any because they are unemployed or do not have any capital. However, those individuals who are unemployed and have no capital need some income to obtain the necessities of life for their subsistence.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Let the government change this old-fashioned way of administering the country and the Canadian people. Let them think of groups of citizens without money and without income before raising the profits and the reserves of institutions, companies, banks and rich people, all of whom are already flourishing economically.
Mr. Chairman the government is still spending its time in promoting productivity, the profits, chances of success, interests and capital surplus of the rich and powerful in Canada, either themselves or their companies. The gap is widening between the rich whose income is increasing and the poor who pay more and more taxes in order to pay for rising interests on public debts. Small wonder that this national imbalance is becoming worse and worse. This must be changed if we want to establish a just society and if we want to have a united Canada.
Have the members of the present government forgotten or, indeed, ever known that companies and individuals can capitalize $28 billion on a production of $68 billion, in 1968, after having lived well and paid their taxes? Have they forgotten or even realized that, at the same time, the government has an administrative deficit every year, and that many citizens and families live from day to day, lacking the necessities of life and cursing the government, progress and society? The government has not thought or ever known what could so easily be done.
Have they ever realized that it would be easy to make a few changes, not within institutions, organizations, banks, companies,
IMr. Latulippe.]
structures and systems, but merely in the basic philosophy of the right hon. Prime Minister, the 29 ministers and the 264 members of the government, so that every citizen who is not working and has no income may be given a share of the revenue of this production of $68 billion in 1968, or out of the capitalization of $28 billion, which is really becoming too ambitious and even harmful and dangerous for the economy.
All you have to do is think about it. The present government can easily set the situation to rights and re-establish economic stability on a nation wide scale.
However, this national economic stability will not come about by itself. It will only be brought about by change; it must be given new directions and steps must be taken to readjust it once more to the actual situation in the country.
Before going any further, I should like to show the graph line of the Liberal budget. The October 24, 1968 edition of La Presse says, and I quote:
Of the eight budgets brought down by the Liberals since they came back into power five years ago, four raised the personal income tax, one reduced it and three left it unchanged.
Since 1963, federal budgets are divided as follows:
June 13, 1963: Mr. Walter Gordon and his "realistic budget" are soon in hot water, and the budget has to be appreciably modified; however, the minister persists in his determination to bring no change in the personal income tax.
April 26, 1965: anticipating a $300 million deficit, Mr. Gordon reduces by 10 per cent the personal income tax. In one year, the government loses $265 million A married man with two children earning $5,000 a year was to benefit from a $30 reduction which brought down to $208 the amount for that fiscal year.
March 29, 1966: Mr. Mitchell Sharp invites the Canadian people to "spread out prosperity". He restores for the most part the reduction granted by Mr. Gordon. The low wage-earners still benefit from a 10 per cent reduction, but on the whole, the government takes back $210 million out of the $265 million lost the previous year. The tax reduction for the taxpayer earning $5,000, now amounts to only $20.
December 19,	1966:	Mr. Sharp's mini-budget
changes the 4 per cent tax on taxable income distinct from the basic tax, tax which pays most of the cost of the old age pension. Increasing from $120 to $240 the maximum amount a taxpayer can pay in that regard, Mr. Sharp increases to $135,000,000 per year the fund which makes it possible to assure an income to pensioners. As a result needy pensioners can get a $30 supplement to their pension which amounted to $75 a month that year.
June 1, 1967: Hoping for a new deficit to fight the recession, Mr. Sharp does not tamper with the income tax rate.

November 3, 1967: Mr. Sharp wants to levy a 5 per cent surtax on basic tax over $100, limiting the increase to $600 for each taxpayer. That bill is defeated in the Commons, and Mr. Sharp proposes a surtax of 3 per cent, illimited, which is finally approved in March of this year.
Effective for 1968 and 1969 only, the surtax will yield $105 million in 12 months. The family-head with a yearly income of $5,000 will have a tax increase of $3.
October 22, 1968: Mr. Benson levies a "social development" tax of 2 per cent which will be effective on January 1, 1989, and which applies to the taxable income, as the old age security tax. Contrary to Mr. Sharp's surtax, this tax does not apply to the basic tax only and, therefore, the yield should be higher. Mr. Benson thinks that this tax of $46 for the taxpayer with an income of $5,000 will yield $440 millions to the government in one year.
That is, Mr. Chairman, the administration, the logic of the present government. The present government is doing eaxctly what its predecessors have done. You do not have to be a genius to understand the situation. Things have not changed an iota in the last five years, the last ten years or even since Confederation. This financial nonsense, Mr. Chairman, adopted in wartime is accepted in peacetime. With the help of borrowed money at exorbitant rates, we are trying to progress in peacetime. In order to pay our wartime debts, we are increasing the value of bonds issued to finance the wars to 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and even 8 percent. Such are the ways of the present administration.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
They imagine themselves able to set things straight, while the economy is tumbling down. There seems to be no ways to find a balance. I think the hon. Minister of Finance is beginning to have headaches. If he would think it over and listen to those who might have some solutions, the situation might improve. I believe it would be easy to decrease the taxes and I believe also that it is easy to have everybody pay taxes on an equal basis rather than having an income tax form for the small taxpayers and one for the others. Under the present system, everything is taken from the poor and given to the rich. If means cannot be found to balance our economy, well, let us take a look at the income tax rates and let justice be done. The most outrageous injustice ever done in any country is found in our income tax rates. It has created widespread dissatisfaction. It is what is bringing on the revolution in Canada and it will lead us to war and disaster. Injustice reigns in the field of taxation.
The Carter report, up to now, has offered logical solutions; however, they have not yet

been followed; they were not even looked into. Like all the other reports, the Carter report will probably remain on the shelf and no attention will be given to it, although it cost $3i millions.
Mr. Chairman, the Berlin or Moscow dictators, as well as the modern banker, grab the people's money and, being dictators, use it either to make guns, or to get people into debt; both types despise mankind, both want to dominate the world. The cult of the race, the cult of the pocket-book, a terrified world, cowering under a deadly weaponry or crushed by ruinous debts which it cannot repay: bend or die, pay or croak, such is the situation and everyone knows it.
Prosperity is not dependent upon a perpetually favourable balance of payments, Mr. Chairman. A monetary instrument does not need gold to play its role. It is unused money that causes unemployment of men, and an injection of new money would revive the general activity. With a currency regulated according to the needs of a country, it would be possible to keep that country out of economic depressions. If the volume of money regulated by the state removes stagnation, money in the hands of the state would guide the various activities and constitute a real dictatorship by the government over the economic life of the country. It would replace bank dictatorship by political dictatorship.
If, on the contrary, Mr. Chairman, by deduction, money originally placed in the hands of the consumer were to guide the economic life, according to the wishes of the consumer, that would generate social and economic democracy where freedom could develop against all forms of planning or dictatorship as imposed upon us today.
As far as workers' salaries and interests paid to investors are concerned, planning will never succeed in solving this problem, since progress is reducing the number of people earning a salary. It is because we cling to that policy of salaries and interests that millions of people earn a bare living and curse progress instead of blessing it. This is why Social Credit is asking to distribute dividends to everybody, so that everybody may share in progress.
I say: "share in progress". Progress is the result of science which, together with the personal work of inventors and investors, who are rewarded in the usual way, which is their justification. But accumulated science, which is common capital, plays an important role in invention and progress. After the capitalist and the inventor, as well as the

Supply-Finance
workers, have been rewarded, that share remains of accumulated science which belongs to everyone.
That is why all the good things which remain unsold, all the good things that the salaries and interests do not buy, belong to everyone. Everyone is entitled to his small share, instead of letting it go to waste and stopping progress. And who is to see that everyone shares in the progress? The present government, seeing it represents everyone and is responsible for the well-being of all.
There are several ways of allowing men to purchase their share of progress. First of all, by lowering the price of goods so that more can be bought per dollar; secondly, by increasing the number of dollars in everyone's hands; thirdly, by lowering the absurdly high rate of interest we are subjected to and tolerate today.
Progress in the volume of production requires progress in the volume of money. As enormous as it is in the first case, it should become enormous in the field of distribution. Those who stick to the old methods of financial distribution, as we do today, are the enemies of progress and distribution; they paralyse the growth of progress in production and prepare the progress of revolution. As progress distinguishes man from the beast, Social Credit distinguishes the intelligent from the imbecile.
The government of a country certainly has the right to administer, legislate, implement for the common good, for the common prosperity of all. The government has that right or, if you would rather, that legal power. It also have the physical power, the executive capacity, it can find the men, the equipment and the things needed to serve the community. But it happens that the government does not acknowledge it has financial power; it always stumbles across restrictions in the field of finance.
This means that in spite of its unquestioned legal power and unlimited physical power, the government stands still for lack of financial power. Even in the case of centralized and planned government, as a result of the bill on economic planning proposed by several honourable members, who are economists too, the same remarks hold true. Legal and physical powers are not enough without financial power.
The honourable minister takes good care to stay away from the financial power. That is why, while proclaiming the rights of each individual, while asking for as much legal

powers as possible for the lower organizations, we maintain that unless a financial power is also given to individuals, corporations and governments, the economy will remain paralysed, plans will stay on the drawing board, certain reports will gather dust, for lack of readers-the minister is aware of that-the citizens will remain poor and unemployment will rise, as is the case today.
At the present time, the number of the unemployed in Canada increases tremendously and within two months, we shall see what happens, as far as unemployment is concerned, in our beautiful Canada.
We do not object to the increase in the price of butter, to a gainful return for the farmers, for their products, but the reasons given by professors of economics are but a recognition of the figures. It is always necessary to adjust man, to adjust the consumer, to adjust the demand to the supply. We always do it the opposite way, and man is the victim.
When will they see the light and adjust the purchasing power? When will the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance bring the purchasing power into line with existing facts and situations? When will we see the great economists, highly paid and highly compensated by the system, ask for reforms in that direction?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief statement with regard to the management of the public debt for the information of the committee and the public in connection with the announcement I am making in the normal way concerning the refunding of forthcoming maturities.
On November 21 I was able to announce the results of the highly successful Canada savings bonds campaign this year, and the plans to refund, through a new issue of $75 million of special 364 day treasury bills, a
November 29, 1968

part of the $125 million of special treasury bills maturing today. These bills were sold at auction yesterday. I am announcing this afternoon plans to refund the $100 million issue of bonds maturing on December 15 and at the same time to refund in advance $100 million of the $400 million of bonds maturing on July 1, 1969. Such advance refunding will be of assistance to us in our debt management operations in the next fiscal year. In addition I have thought it prudent to raise an additional $50 million in cash through this issue to cover a portion of the recent increase in our exchange reserves, which will be announced in accordance with the usual timetable on Tuesday morning next.
I think it may be helpful to review the present prospect for further public debt operations during the remainder of the current fiscal year. In doing so I must stress the tentative nature of our projections by reason of unforeseeable changes in our foreign exchange reserves and also in the pace of the normal seasonal redemptions of outstanding Canada savings bonds.
Over the remaining four months of the present fiscal year I may wish to make some modest increase in the volume of treasury bills outstanding. Such an increase would take the form of small additions from time to time in the regular weekly issue of 91 day and 182 day bills. Combined with the bond financing announced today a modest increase in the bill issue, on present expectations, would leave the government with adequate working balances at the end of the fiscal year. In mid March plans will be announced for the refunding of $410 million of marketable bonds maturing on April 1. It is quite possible that this financing will be designed to raise some new money to meet the seasonal decline in cash balances in April. As in the issue announced today, the possibility of advance refunding will be considered in connection with each new issue to facilitate the orderly phasing of our debt management program.

Mr. Chairman, while I am on my feet I should like to comment very briefly on a few matters which were raised by hon. members opposite. First of all, I wish to return to the question of the recent developments in the international monetary system, which has been raised by the hon. Leader of the Opposition. The recent crisis which affected the Deutsche mark, the French franc, and indirectly other currencies as well, was a source of deep concern. We can therefore all be reassured by the development in the exchange market during the past week. The measures announced by Germany, France and the United Kingdom, and the evidence of their vigorous implementation, appear to have restored the stability to the foreign exchange situation. A good start has been made.
It is understandable, however, that a disturbance on the scale of the past fortnight has given rise to some questions about the monetary system itself. On November 25, members of this house suggested that the system should be re-examined once again by an international conference. Similar suggestions have been heard from a number of other quarters and, in particular, the suggestion has been made that there should be a greater degree of flexibility in exchange rates.
I believe it would be appropriate for me to stress that the attitude of the government of Canada toward the international monetary system has been far from rigid. Members are familiar with the many discussions which have taken place in a variety of international meetings in recent years. During the last five years in particular, those concerned with international monetary question have met regularly within the framework of such organizations as the I.M.F., the Group of Ten and O.E.C.D. Canada has participated actively from the outset in all of these discussions, seeking to find ways of improving the system and consistently supporting the great number of improvements which have resulted.
The most notable of these has been the scheme for special drawing rights. It is hoped that the enlargement of the powers of the International Monetary Fund to allocate special drawing rights, which will add to international liquidity in a manner subject to rational, international control, will soon be an accomplished fact. In this context members might wish to note the significance of the forthcoming amendments to the Bretton Woods agreement legislation, which will enable Canada to help achieve this goal at an

November 29, 1968
Supply-Finance
early date. Improvements have also been made in the arrangements regarding gold. Less spectacular, perhaps, but at least as important, have been the continuing efforts to improve the balance of payments policies of countries, and the operation of the adjustment process. Canada will continue to participate in his process of evolution and will examine with interest every proposal for further improvement of the system. The advantages and disadvantages of such particular proposals as that to enlarge the permitted degree of exchange rate flexibility are debatable. I feel some concern that the recent monetary difficulties may cause our attention to be diverted from the progress which has been achieved in international trade and payments in recent decades. During the postwar period world trade has grown rapidly and has been liberalized to a very marked degree. This has been of great benefit to Canada as a major trading nation whose prosperity depends on world trade to a degree equalled by few, if any other countries. It also was achieved, despite the fact that international liquidity grew at a much less rapid rate, particularly so in recent years.
Imbalances have emerged and have occasionally given rise to crises. These difficulties, however, have been contained by the adoption of appropriate economic and financial policies by industrial countries and, in the short run, by international support operations, all of which evolved within the framework of international consultations. I might refer in this context to the substantial improvement in the balance of payments of the United States which recent statistics have indicated. The first order of business therefore is to press on with these tasks and implement the plans which have been made to ensure future growth of international reserves.
