The high priced officials who assist the minister are in the gallery, and I am sure the Minister of Finance would be happy to table those independent reports that some of his officials may have prepared on the effect of implementing Carter's recommendations on the economic growth in Canada. In any event, perhaps the minister can be persuaded to show those reports prepared by members of his department to hon. members of the house.
It will be remembered that the minister of finance of that time invited different corporations to present briefs, setting September 30 as the deadline. Amazingly, 100 briefs came from industry alone. I have it on good authority that International Nickel spent $250,000 preparing their brief to fight the Carter report. When a hundred corporations attempt to justify their positions, one cannot but become suspicious. As my hon. friend says it is a clear attempt to preserve socialism for the rich.
November 29, 1988

[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In October, 1967, the minister promised a white paper containing tax proposals as close to the end of the year as possible-he did not indicate which year. This white paper has still to be produced. Some time in 1968 it was decided to drop this idea of a white paper. Now, the present Minister of Finance tells us we may see these long-awaited tax proposals in the early part of 1969, and that some of them may be implemented by the end of 1969. From the time this report was tabled by the government, back in February, 1967, some 20 months have now passed. One might ask: how much has this cost Canadians? One economist has calculated that this failure on the part of the government to act promptly on the proposals has cost Canadians a thousand dollars a minute, or roughly half a billion dollars a year. If this is so, there is certainly a strong case for deciding not to implement this proposed 2 per cent social improvement tax which the minister so proudly announced on budget night. If Canadians are losing all this money through failure to implement the Carter recommendations, it is high time he took some action to do so.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Carter made particular studies of certain areas of taxation. On the question of oil companies he told us they got one third of their profits tax-free on the ground that their assets, their underground assets, were being depleted. Profits from new mines are tax-free for the first three years-most oil well and gas costs are tax deductible. Mr. Carter said this cost the treasury $150 million a year in lost revenues. Some of the potash companies in the west have attempted to take advantage of this tax holiday. I am told they work for a while on exploration or development, and when the end of the three-year period is approaching they form new companies and attempt to get another three-year tax holiday. I should like to hear a statement from the minister with regard to the actions of some of these companies, most of which are attempting, not to evade the law but to avoid it.
In the year 1964, Mr. Carter said, eight big companies three of which were oil companies, accounted for 85 per cent of all depletion allowances in Canada. Because of heavy foreign ownership of our resources, United States residents received 80 per cent of the oil and mining benefits. Mr. Carter also told us that small businessmen have an easy time with the tax man because they pay only 21 per cent on the first $35,000 of their profits.
Supp ly-Finance
On the face of it, the government is soaking the big-income boys because the tax rate on incomes above $400,000 is 80 per cent. But, as the Carter report makes clear, tax rates as high as this are in practice only on the statute books; they are readily avoided by most of the few people who receive incomes of this size. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, the tearful plea made by the Prime Minister for those who are paying 80 per cent. He told us down in Halifax that he would have to take care of these people because otherwise we might see a flight of these talented men to other countries. He was not so much worried about the difficulties the little people might find in paying this 2 per cent social welfare tax, but he was concerned about these 80 per cent boys. I think we ought to draw Mr. Carter's words, that such a rate exists "only on the statute books", not only to the Minister of Finance but also to the Prime Minister.
Present practice under taxation law is to place the emphasis on the word "avoidance" rather than on the word "evasion". If ever avoidance is being exercised by corporations, it is within our Canadian tax structure. I happen to be a lawyer, and I might add that lawyers seem to do quite well in persuading big corporations to take advantage of this angle of avoidance.
Talking about people with incomes of $400,000 and more a year, this is one of the sleek methods they use to avoid taxation. They acquire farms and attempt to say they are in the farming business. Then they apply all the expenses of the farm operation-which in many cases runs at a loss-against income. After a few years have gone by, they have acquired a large tract of land, and taking advantage of urban expansion are able to dispose of it for a large capital gain. The minister in charge of housing is here, and he knows that this is the case. They have it both going and coming, as my hon. friend says.
I should like to spend a few minutes, now, considering the question of a capital gains tax. Yesterday I noticed that according to the Daily Star the premier of Ontario is studying the idea of a land profit tax. The article in the Star reads as follows:
The Ontario government is considering a capital gains tax on land speculation, Premier John Robarts told the legislature yesterday.
The tax would bolster revenue in the face of a government austerity program and help ease the high cost of housing in Ontario cities.
Robarts said the treasury board is currently examining all areas of taxation "and this is one of them."

November 29, 1968
Supply-Finance
If this is one of the areas which the government of Ontario is studying, it is high time not only the Minister of Finance but the minister in charge of housing paid attention. If we permit the provincial governments to step in with regard to a capital gains tax the hon. gentleman will have a difficult time with his task force on housing, should it bring forward reasonable recommendations to solve the housing problem. It is one of the real shortcomings of Canadian tax history that we should have no capital gains tax. Such a tax exists in the United States and in Britain, yet in Canada we do nothing about those who speculate in land or who devote themselves to the stock market and make huge profits with which they escape tax free.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
When I heard the speech of the hon. member for Scarborough East who, by the way, is an economist and was one of the whiz kids who advised former minister of finance Walter Gordon when he introduced that great budget of his a few years ago, I thought our present Minister of Finance would pay some attention to him. In the budget debate the hon. member strongly urged that we have a capital gains tax. I suggest that the minister read his speech and learn from it. These are some of the aspects upon which I would like the minister to comment. He has about seven minutes before this debate adjourns, and I have raised seven matters with him. I am sure he can touch on at least some of them.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister when we are going to get a draft bill?
Mr. Chairman, I shall take that under advisement. I cannot make a promise without first talking to my officials.
I just want to emphasize again that I do not see any real excuse for the state of uncertainty in which people are being left.

Sometimes these questions drag on and we do not get the estimates back again for several more days. In that way it is a little awkward to keep track of them.

Would the minister care to answer the questions that hon. members put to him?

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the hon. member was not here put I answered the questions put forward by many speakers this afternoon. I believe the last speaker is the only one whose questions I have not answered, and they were of such a general nature that they are difficult to answer. First of all he asked if I am in favour of a floating exchange rate. My answer is no. To me it is rather unusual to see this new alliance between the N.D.P. and the president of the Royal Bank.
The other questions raised were very general ones about what we are going to do in connection with the Carter report and other submissions that the government has had on taxation. Of course I am not going to indicate what we intend to do until I produce the draft bill which will be studied by all members of the house.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should let this item pass at this time. I wish to raise one or two things before the hour of five o'clock. In the last few days I have been going over some of the old Hansards. We learn a lot from history, but it is said that quite frequently those of us who live at the present time do not take too much cognizance of what has gone before.
I went back to 1962 and read some of the statements made by the Minister of Finance during the budget debate of that year when another party was in power.
I must tell him I thoroughly enjoyed reading the words of wisdom which he addressed to the House of Commons on a number of occasions, and the thought occurred to me that surely all the good ideas he had in those days cannot have gone by the board since he assumed the august position of finance minister in the federal government.
I am going to relate his old ideas to just one phase of one operation in my home province of British Columbia, and I am going to refer to the big coal operation around Vernon, the Kaiser coal operation. The minister is well aware of what has happened. The former company, Crowsnest Industries, has sold out to Kaiser Steel which has bought a large area of coal from that company. Kaiser have moved in and they are going to set up a strip mining operation. As I recall the minister's remarks he was not too happy about big, foreign owned companies moving into areas such as this in the field of natural resources
November 29, 1968

and getting special tax concessions-for example, a three year exemption period on mining.
I ask the minister, is your department going to allow the Kaiser corporation a three year tax exemption period in this particular operation? Here is a loophole that could and should be plugged by the federal government. All over this country of ours we have big corporations that get these tax concessions. I can give several good examples. They get an initial tax concession. Then they set up a new company, move over a short distance and get another tax concession for another three year period. They are robbing the public of Canada of hundreds of millions of dollars that rightfully should be going into the tax coffers of the federal government.
This was the line which the minister took several years ago in connection with oil and gas reserves in the Dominion of Canada. He pointed out that we were forced to import 50 per cent or more of our oil requirements, and emphasized what a drain this was on the financial resources of the country. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I ask him what are you going to do about it now? You are sitting in the seat where you can do a job. What recommendations are you going to make to the cabinet and to the House of Commons? Are you, Mr. Minister of Finance, going to suggest that we alter this approach? If so, it is up to you to lay before the house within the next two or three months some changes which will bring your old ideas to fruition.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-ll, to govern, licence and regulate the operation of rainmaking equipment in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, had I known the date when this bill would be called we probably could have tied it in with the Grey Cup game and the rain situation in Toronto. Probably a number of people would have been

November 29, 1968
Rainmaking Equipment very interested in supporting this bill. That of course is no joke, because on a number of occasions the company operating out of Montreal has been asked to project the weather on a longer term basis to decide whether there would be snow, rain, or what the weather would be, when Grey Cup game time came around, especially a crucial game.
I, and I am sure other members, have been interested in two or three things connected with a bill of this nature. One is the attitude of people to a bill called a bill to regulate rainmaking. I am sure many people still think of the Indian dances that are being performed in Arizona and sold to tourists as representing the former method of rainmaking.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LICENSING AND REGULATION
speechtext: And in the west.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LICENSING AND REGULATION
speechtext:
Yes. They may have one in the west. It might be interesting for the hon. member, who comes from Saskatchewan, to know that his friends, the farmers in Alberta, over a period have voted, in a number of districts, that a certain amount of money be paid, through taxes to rainmakers to make rain in that area, and more important to end hail in that area. While this also may be considered to have dubious value, those farmers have renewed this proposition for many years now in the province of Alberta and are very close to having the provincial government make a decision in respect of everybody paying taxes so that hail does not occur in that area.
The whole matter of rainmaking involves a very large problem of weather modification and what the international and national relationship to this should be. It is quite clear, in a broad sense, that in the foreseeable future we will be able not only to plot weather fronts of various kinds throughout the world by satellite control but that we will also be able, through several methods that are being developed, to prevent what would be the disadvantages of those storm fronts developing. This will happen where expenditures are made to control hurricanes, fog, hail, and I suggest probably to control or modify the normal rainfall in a given area. All these things are being undertaken. If we in Canada think this is a joke, then we should look at the situation in the United States. In the year 1967 in the United States $7 million was spent on this type of weather control. It is expected by 1970 the expenditure will be $150 million. That is equivalent to the total amount spent by the Canadian government a few years ago

on its total works on behalf of all the people in Canada.
I suggest it is necessary that we pay some attention to the matter of weather control. Frankly I am interested in a very small sphere of weather control; that is, the ability of people by certain processes to make rain fall in a given area in greater amounts than would normally be the case if the weather were uncontrolled. I suggest that in Ontario we have engaged in this for some time. We have seen the Ontario department of agriculture contribute a quarter of a million dollars to make rain in the Renfrew area, when that area experienced a severe drought. You will also be aware, Mr. Speaker, that in the same area money was spent by the Ontario Department of Agriculture to compensate the people for an over-abundance of rain in that fall period. You may also believe that there is something to rainmaking by noise, because you will remember a few years ago while the noise was being made in parliament it started to rain in the Renfrew area. That foreshadowed the end of that drought and preceded the bringing in of generators by about three days.
There may be many methods by which this can be done. I am not particular how we do it. However, I believe it would be a shame if members of parliament do not take some action in this matter, because it would seem to me that we must be able to protect the people who now are the victims of modification of weather, and really have no control over it. If someone decided to dust the apple trees in his yard with a heavy spray, and this covered the yard next door, then the person next door is protected because there is legislation which provides that something can be done about this. He may have his grass replaced or his flowers replaced because of the over-kill by the spraying of the person two lots down the street. So long as the Canadian parliament takes the attitude that this is a big joke nothing will happen.
For a change the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) is here. We are glad to see him in the house. This does concern the Minister of Transport because I believe it will have to be his responsibility. An agency is hired by his department to assist in long range weather forecasting. His department has a responsibility for this forecasting. It is my opinion that his department will also have to be involved in the matter of weather modification.
November 29, 1968

I do not suggest that the department of lands and forests in northern Ontario should not be able to hire silver oxide machines to bring about water precipitation in a given area. What I do suggest, however, is that if this affects some people living in that area they should have recourse through law for the recovery of damages suffered by them in that regard.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LICENSING AND REGULATION
speechtext: I have listened to the hon. member's contention about the rights of people to recourse as a result of the adverse effects of provincial activity in rainmaking. How can this be done under the type of provisions he is putting before the house? Is there not a grave constitutional problem involved here? Does his own legislation not exempt provincial activity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LICENSING AND REGULATION
speechtext:
Yes, there is a major problem here. In the United States they have done some work in this regard and have come across similar problems. They have listed a number of basic questions regarding control in this respect. Some of them are:
How should the regulatory function be performed? Can an agency with mission interests in weather modification serve also as a national licensing and regulatory authority? Is a new agency necessary for this purpose? Can the co-ordinating function and the regulatory function be combined in a single agency? Is it premature to undertake federal licensing and regulation?
The United States has passed a number of laws in respect of weather modification as a result of their investigations in this matter. I understand the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) has also done some research in this regard. Weather control really involves weather projections. Weather conditions are projected not only in respect of Newfoundland but in respect of British Columbia, and these projections are made simultaneously. These are made without any provincial control or provincial information. They are also based on international information.
I am sure everyone is impressed when watching television to see that satellites thousands of miles above the earth project back pictures of weather formation. We no longer see lines drawn to indicate weather fronts; we now see the actual fronts. This is done not only on a national basis, but on an international basis; so one should not worry too
Rainmaking Equipment much about the provincial implications. Weather modification is not confined to provincial jurisdictions. Anything that crosses provincial boundaries becomes national in nature. Therefore I believe we should not hesitate to make laws in this field simply because provinces have a role to play.
A number of laws have already been passed in the United States in this regard, but one problem they have experienced relates to the fact that the laws in one state often conflict with those in another. In any event, they have been able to establish a number of facts, one of which is that rainmaking must naturally come under governmental regulations. This authority goes on to state that weather is national in scope rather than a state proposition. In this regard a number of cases have been heard in both district or state and federal courts. This is an extensive field, and I believe our federal government must have some control.
The hon. member's question has more relationship to the making of rain than to the powers or authorities I recommend. I refer only to control and regulation by licence. There are only seven or eight companies of this kind operating in this field. Surely we could regulate them as to the weather modifications they may carry out. In this way we could require these companies to keep a record of the results of their attempts.
The main example we have in this country is in respect of the firm Weather Engineering which is operated by Paul Denison and Bernard Power of Montreal. They have had great success with the silver iodide generators. These are small coke operated ovens in which you place crystals of silver iodide. The temperature is brought up to about 1,200 or 1,400 degrees. The iodide cystals are evaporated and go up into the clouds by convection. When the clouds are supercooled, usually about 10 degrees fahrenheit, the iodide crystals create a molecular bond which attracts the moisture in the air. This produces precipitation in the form of rain or snow. If this is in a cold area snow will fall, which eventually can turn to rain. Whether or not these efforts have been successful can be judged by what has happened.
Let me refer to what happened in 1956. There was some talk about using this system to control forest fires in northern Ontario. The article to which I refer states:
In Quebec the clouds held more moisture. In mid-July, for example, a forest fire out of control along a ten mile front in the wild North Shore

November 29, 1968
Rainmaking Equipment Paper Co. bushland, southwest of Seven Islands, was rapidly sweeping toward the little St. Lawrence settlement of Shelter Bay.
Denison and Power flew in 23 of their silver iodide generators. On the morning of July 22 a few weak storm clouds drifted over the blaze but produced no rainfall. At noon Denison ordered his fireboxes lit. By five o'clock 1.3 inches of rain had fallen on the blazing timber-enough to dampen down the smoke and enable forest rangers to close in on the flames. The showers quenched the fire just in time to save Shelter Bay. The community was already partly evacuated and flames had reached some of its outlying buildings. Said H. A. Sewell, Quebec North Shore's general manager of woodlands, "We have seen enough of the work of Power and Denison to know that we want more."
On October 7, 12,000 crackling dry square miles of Abitibi Power and Paper Co. forest from Lake Abitibi west to Kapuskasing, Ont., were drenched with 2.8 inches of rain a few hours after Denison's generators went into action. Some small fires fizzled out and, for the first time in months, rivers rose to normal levels, hydro plants began operating at full capacity and reservoirs started to fill up, giving hope of adequate water storage before freeze-up.
Denison called George Arnold, chief chemist of Spruce Falls Power and Paper Co., at Kapuskasing one Sunday in September, advising him to alert company forest rangers operating Weather Engineering silver iodide furnaces. Rain-heavy clouds were passing over Spruce Falls forests the next morning.
We must remember that he was in Montreal, a thousand miles away from Kapuskasing, yet he said:
"Light your generators at seven o'clock and keep them burning until eleven," he instructed. It started to rain on Monday morning at a quarter to eight. The shower stopped abruptly at half past eleven. Bushlands surrounding the Spruce Falls property didn't get the downpour. The government weather office had forecast no rain for the region until Wednesday.
I am convinced that you can make rain. We have had some very bad seasons in northern Ontario when we had no forest fires at all, yet the department of lands and forests were operating these machines.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The same was true when Ontario Hydro decided to fill their reservoirs. It may be that we want to make a rainshed out of the whole of northern Ontario, but if we do, those people who are already there in the field of tourism and agriculture, and in fact those people who live there, should be able to have a say in the matter and to start litigation in the courts if they consider the effects to be detrimental to them.
I suggest that this is a responsibility of the federal government which it should exercise.

If the members of this house wish to pursue this matter, they could vote to have the bill referred to a committee. I suggest it should be studied by officials of the Department of Transport, which has a very large meteorological service, of which we should be proud. This weather institute, which operates in Montreal, has a direct teletype communication with the Department of Transport. It plots the weather in its Montreal offices and then sells the weather forecasts back to agencies, such as Air Canada and others, in a completely different form. The two specialists at the institute have been trained by the Canadian government and are familiar with its methods. They are able to forecast from maps well ahead of time the type of storm fronts that are likely to develop under given circumstances and from given areas.
For instance, if you, Mr. Speaker, wanted to select a nice day for your daughter's wedding because you wanted to hold it in the garden, you could consult these experts who would be able to provide you with the information, so that you could select a day of sunshine and suitable temperature for the event. For businessmen these experts can provide a correct forecast with reasonable certainty. They are able to say whether or not the use of dry ice or silver iodide which is being discharged by artillery will be successful in producing rain.
We in this house will be failing in our duty toward people who live in areas where rain can be produced, or toward government agencies which need to control weather, if we do not soon take a look at the whole matter of weather modification, and provide regulations and licences necessary for these people to operate in this field.
My purpose in producing this bill is to ensure that such agencies as the Department of Agriculture, Ontario and Quebec hydro, private pulp and paper mills and other agencies interested in this field do not abuse a new technology which, as is not realized by most people, is involved in the modification of weather, an undertaking in which all civilized countries are now engaged, in one way or another.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LICENSING AND REGULATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take the floor on the bill now under consideration. We had planned to introduce such a bill but I think the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) read
November 29, 1968

our minds, and I congratulate him for having introduced that bill.
It will first of all have the advantage of finally convincing everyone that artificial rain exists. In fact, many people still do not believe it, but I can say that our regions had a taste of it, so to speak, because we had to put up with uncontrolled artificial rain during three summers and that is why I support that bill.
It is not that I am against artificial rain, Mr. Speaker; not at all. But I am in favour of artificial rain controlled by legislation, so that the government will know to whom permits are delivered, but most of all the permits will state exactly the regions where artificial rain can be made, as well as when it can be made, to prevent what happened in our regions.
Rain is being made throughout the summer without regard to planting or harvesting. That is the reason why our areas have been flooded during three consecutive summers by this artificial rain.
I remember five or six years ago when we raised this question of rainmaking in the house, we had started a roar of laughter in the house. Now I understand why hon. members felt that was rather funny. In fact, the government was aware of rainmaking experiments, but they considered them a military secret. I do not think that they should be so considered, because if rainmaking is interesting to big companies-as it has been for some years-it is even more interesting to farmers.
The matter also concerns the population for reasons of public health. Excesses should not occur again as in the past years, when Operation Umbrella was launched in the Saguenay-Lake St. John area. Everybody was crying for help, and I think it influenced very much the reports of doctors who appeared as witnesses and stated that this could affect the health of the population.
Legislation should be passed to grant permits to a company, but that company should not be solely in the service of large corporations. In my opinion, the legislation should provide that the companies would come under the government control, because if we let them act as they please, the abuses will continue.
On the one hand, we hear the opinion of the farmers or of the people. The population of a given region knows and realizes that the
Rainmaking Equipment government may at certain times allow companies to make artificial rain in order to raise the water level of hydraulic reservoirs, but that it will see to it, at the same time, that this rain does not drown the crops planted by the farmers or spoil the grain or the hay harvest.
Mr. Speaker, I wish with all my hearts that this legislation may be refered to a committee for consideration, so that the government might, if necessary, introduce legislation to that effect for the situation is urgent. I have proof of that here, for I have a whole file on this question of artificial rain. It would take me nearly a week to read all the evidence in favour of or against artificial rain, and all of it proves to the Canadian people and to all the hon. members that artificial rain has been in existence for many years.
At first, ground rainmaking machines were used. Today, however, planes are used to seed clouds. In our areas, ground machines are hardly used any more, because it is much easier to use airplanes. That is why the matter today concerns the federal government far more than provincial governments, because it is a question of air pollution. When ground rain-making machines were used, the matter concerned the provincial governments. I always wondered why the government has been hiding that fact from the people for the past ten years. Why can the government not reveal when companies will be allowed to make rain? If one region is not suited for such a program the people will be in a position to advise the government as to its ill effects.
Mr. Speaker, I was anxious to have this bill discussed in order to bring in the final proof. This latest testimony we received from the C.F.U. on August 30, 1968; as you see, it is recent enough. I will not have the time to read this letter entirely as I would not want to have this bill killed today so that it may be referred to a committee. I will read a few excerpts.
Dear Sir, as a result of the decisions taken during our annual convention concerning the effects of bad weather upon our members, as well as upon the whole population of the Saguenay-Lac St-Jean district, and considering the possibility that artificial rainmaking may be the cause, the Federation de I'UCC du Saguenay is requesting your assistance to set matters straight in the minds of our population and to find out whether artificial rainmaking is being practised at the present time. If it were practised, please help us to get rid, once and for all, of this disastrous system which caused us untold hardships some years ago.

November 29, 1968
Rainmaking Equipment
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I feel that the C.F.U. might have laid it a bit thick, as such an organization cannot really be 100 percent against all experiments in cloud seeding. It probably hopes for restrictions in a particular region at a given time, as I said previously.
Our farmers and our population as a whole could not endure the consequences of artificial rainmaking; more over, uncertainty about this condition is unbearable.
In the past, ground rainmaking machines have been used in our province and in our region.
A great number of those machines were used in the northern part of the province of Quebec. There were some in our region, in St-Felix d'Otis, Shipshaw, Falardeau, Chfite-aux-Galets, etc.
All the places where ground rainmaking machines were used are listed. I happen to have a map indicating the site of all those machines.
The services were engaged by the Association Protectrice des Forets Laurentiennes Ltee, as well as by hydro-electric companies, including Hydro-Quebec after the nationalisation of power production.
The Department of Land and Forests of the province also contributed financially to that operation, through the Association Protectrice des Forets Laurentiennes.
Following pressures by the UCC, the news media and Operation Umbrella, the provincial government assured the UCC, through the Minister of Natural Resources, that Hydro Quebec would stop using the services of the Weather Engineering Limited (Meteorological Engineering) and it asked the Gatineau Power as well as the Association de protection des Forets laurentiennes, the other two sponsors at that time, not to resume cloud seeding operations. Moreover, the minister undertook to supply the C.F.U. with the list of the places where the seeding machines were located to afford better supervision.
And it is on that occasion that we secured a map showing the exact location of the machines.
Since then, the C.F.U has kept in touch with the senior officials of the Department of Natural Resources in order to maintain pressure to prevent cloud seeding. In addition, each time serious information was received, it sent its technicians to check if there was anything to it.
However, it is impossible for a union group to survey the Quebec territory to find rainmaking equipment, when one knows that this equipment is very small and can easily be disguised.
With new developments, the federal government got involved.
Now, especially during the last five or six years, rainmaking is carried out by airplanes and this is precisely what C.F.U. is referring to.
On July 28, 1967, the federal government, through the Air Transport Board, granted Royalair Ltd. an air survey licence (rainmaking).

Nobody dared to say that that was a rainmaking licence; they said it was for air survey, but it was, in fact for rainmaking.
In its argument to the board, Royalair Ltd. said that it wanted to operate in conjunction with Weather Engineering. We also had confirmation, during the public hearing of the Air Transport Board that Ontario Hydro, Abitibi Corporation and Spruce Falls Paper Company resorted to artificial seeding of clouds in order to increase rainfall. We also had confirmation, on that occasion, that Newfoundland was also a victim of that cloud seeding by the Newfoundland Air Transport Limited Company.
Therefore, to that method of cloud seeding from the ground, is added that of seeding by aircraft.
Faced with this reality, the annual convention of the Saguenay C.F.U., which was held on August 31,	1967, officially and publicly reaffirmed its
position as follows:
(1)	That the provincial and federal governments, within their respective jurisdiction, should make the necessary arrangements so as to maintain the ban on all the methods which might increase natural rainfall in our area and that the state should exercise a strict control in that respect.
(2)	That the state should undertake a serious and complete study of the influence on our climate of the numerous and large underground streams artificially created by hydroelectric dams and the consequences these may have on farming, so as to take them into account in the planning of our agriculture.
The position of the C.F.U. Federation is just as unequivocal. In fact, the resolution passed at the last general convention of the C.F.U. held in Quebec City in October 1967, read as follows:
The general convention of the C.F.U. recommends to the federal and provincial governments to revoke immediately all licences issued for cloud seeding.
I think the C.F.U. is suggesting that we should ask some questions so as to get further information on orders of the day. That is what I did. I am waiting for answers to my questions. All this should bring the government to pass legislation. We must have some legislation and we can no longer leave this matter up to some companies. Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable to say this, but during the past years, I even read articles written by the authorities of certain companies defending these seedings. They stated that the interests of companies and industries should come before the interest of the population.
For my part, I say that this is absolutely false. We are here in the first place to work for the population without neglecting the industrial interests and especially research, but it is possible I think to associate both, to protect the population and carry on such research, because as the hon. member for
November 29, 1968

Timiskaming stated earlier, this is scientific progress which could be quite valuable in case of a disaster and could even improve the production of our industries. We should not stop everything by saying: We do not want any more seeding. No. Once again I insist that we merely want that seeding to be governed by a specific act which will take into account all the interested parties. We plead the case of the people, but company officials, just like farmers, also have the right to plead their own case.
This bill is a start and if perchance it is not referred to a committee this evening, I would urge the government to introduce similar legislation right after the Christmas recess. Mr. Speaker, the house may rest assured that we will support it, thereby expressing the will of all those who, in the past, have suffered from those artificial rains because they were not controlled. Cloud seeding without control is like anything else which may be good in itself but becomes evil when there is any excess.
I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, in order not to prolong the debate any more-I would not want to be accused of having killed the bill- that the bill will be referred to a committee for study and that legislation will be introduced for the control of cloud seeding as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) says he believes there are effective rainmaking machines and the bill appears to be based upon that premise. This is a subject that has long vexed the south-central area of Alberta, that I have the honour to represent. I noticed the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) intervened in the debate, I suppose because of his connection with the same area. Everyone in that area is extremely interested in this question of weather modification. Despite long studies and a great deal of money that is being spent in a study of the subject by individuals, private groups, municipalities, provincial governments and federal government agencies, it has certainly not become clear to the population of Alberta or to the government of that province that there are such things as effective rainmaking machines. In fact, the large groups of population in that area are divided into those who belong to the converted and those who belong to the unconverted in regard to weather modification.
Rainmaking Equipment
Every year,	Mr. Speaker, we find
municipalities subjected to plebiscites to determine whether or not they should pass a bylaw to enable them to employ the services of a weather modification company. I might say that the most prominent company in this regard is the Irving P. Creek Company based in California, who have operated their fans in Alberta.
Some people have adopted weather modification almost as a religion. Others are equally as well convinced that the theory of it is inaccurate and that it is ineffective. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, there is an annual plebiscite conducted at great expense in the municipalities involved. The subject creates bad feeling between neighbours, and we cannot seem to come to any final conclusion as to whether or not the provincial government, at least, should recognize the procedure as an effective one.
It is my feeling that instead of passing a bill such as this, which does not seem to promote the kind of inquiry required into this general field-as I have said, the situation is not fully clarified as yet-the government should be devoting its activities to promoting more research in this area. In this respect I feel that the bill is premature.
I know my hon. friends who sit in the same part of the house as the sponsor of the bill are very prone to controlling things; it seems that that is their expertise. But in this case they will not even allow the goose to be born, before wanting to control what might be the goose that lays the golden egg.
If there is indeed some method by which rain can be increased in the prairie provinces, then the output of the area could be doubled or tripled. Large areas of eastern Alberta, and I suppose western Saskatchewan, are not producing the crops they could produce if they received more rain.
The explanatory note to the bill says the purpose of the bill is to provide for compensation where damage is deemed to result from the use of rainmaking machines. I have looked through the bill but I cannot see this provision. I find no clause in it which lays responsibility for damage caused. It does not say that the government or that the user of the machine will be responsible for such damage.

Until such a thing happens we are dealing with something, really, that is not here. I suggest we have no effective machines and we cannot control them. I think the government would be better advised to undertake research into this subject.

If we could produce such machines the agricultural output of this nation would be greatly increased. Frankly, everyone in my area would be happy to settle this question, since feuds are developing over it.
I do not think the bill should be referred to committee; I think it is premature, and this is the wrong way to attack the problem. That there is a problem I agree, but the answer to it lies in research, and not in some sort of legislation which seeks to control machines which have not proven effective.

Mr. Speaker, this is one of those rare occasions when I find myself agreeing with the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I told him today I wanted to speak on the subject because I think there ought to be some kind of control over rainmaking equipment. A few years ago I would have put rainmaking machines into the category occupied by voodoo and witch doctors. After spending the last summer in northern Ontario I have changed my mind, because we were rained out in northern Ontario.
I understand that the entire subject is of large scope and has been studied by the meteorological branch. I know that complicated policy implications are involved, and that rainmaking machines are still experimental.

Frankly, I cannot understand all the fuss about constitutional problems that was raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). These machines came into use without anyone raising constitutional problems. It seems, though, that when it is a question of buckets of water falling on the heads of my people in northern Ontario we have to be involved in constitutional matters to stop it.
The Northeastern Ontario Municipal Association met at the end of the summer and sent me a letter, which I assume other hon. members received also. The association wants the senior or federal government to pass legislation controlling weather modification apparatus. The association represents 17 municipalities in northeastern Ontario and says this in its letter:
As you are aware, the heavy rainfall which occurred in this area, leaves a lot to be desired, and has caused damages to our tourist and wood industries, and farmers.
The attached figures compare rainfalls for the summer months of 1967 and 1968. In June, 1967, there were 3.37 inches of rainfall, for this year, 1968, the rainfall was almost double, at 6.09 inches. In July 1967, average rainfall was 2.8 inches and in July of this year it was 8.97 inches. I think this indicates conclusively that rainmaking machines are effective.
The explanatory note of the bill has this to say, in part:
It appears that control licensing and regulations must be adapted to protect the public and make possible the payment of compensation where damage is deemed to result from such use.
I do not think you could apply such legislation, since rainmaking equipment is not like a switch. It will not rain when you press the switch, and stop raining when you take your finger off the switch. Therefore it will not be possible to make compensation. One would have to go to court and prove that the damage caused resulted directly from rain brought on by rainmaking machines, and I do not see how that would be possible.
I should prefer to see a bill that seeks only to control these machines, so that not just any company, or any Tom, Dick or Harry could try to make rain. What would happen, for example, if one of these machines went out of control? Supposing someone seeded clouds and it began to rain uncontrollably? What if our weather were affected over a long term? All that ought to be considered. I think that studies ought to be undertaken in this field.
